channel.title: ENN | Egui News Network
channel.description: ENN | Egui News Network reports from Japan on the side of Japanese history and culture that schools never teach: the plots, the scandals, the executions and the quiet deals behind the beautiful image of Japan. If you love Japan, this is the Japan behind the postcard, told straight in plain English. Read the full stories on Substack, and get the collected editions as books on Amazon.

item.title: World War II: The War Decided by Resources, Not Courage (1939-1945)
item.description: On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes wrecked the American battle fleet at Pearl Harbor in about two hours. It was one of the most brilliant surprise attacks in history. Six months later, at Midway, Japan lost four aircraft carriers in a few days. America lost one carrier there, and then built more than one hundred new carriers during the war. Japan could never replace its four. Brave men fought and died on both sides, in fleets, in jungles, and in burning cities. But the result was already hidden in shipyards, oil fields, and lists of allies. This war was won by the side that could build, fuel, and feed more than the other. The Second World War split the world into two armed camps, the Axis and the Allies. The Axis won many early battles with speed, skill, and surprise. But victory in the long war went to resources, production, and alliances, not to courage alone. Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/second-world-war/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/7S0X0q7P1gQ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Second Sino-Japanese War Explained: The War Japan Started With No Way to End It
item.description: In 1937, Japan started a war in China that it never formally declared. Its leaders expected a short fight and a quick settlement within months. Eight years later, that war was still going on, and Japan was still stuck inside it. By then it had spread across China and pulled in a second, even larger war against America. Millions of Chinese soldiers and civilians were dead, and hundreds of thousands of Japanese soldiers were dead too. Japan began a war with no decided ending, and then found that it could not end it. Japan went to war in 1937 without deciding what victory would look like or when the fighting should stop. China refused to surrender, moved its capital deep inland, and kept fighting from a country too vast to occupy. Stuck in that quagmire, Japan hunted for resources and supply routes further south, and that hunt pushed it toward war with America. Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/second-sino-japanese-war/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/6IRzVTSHdVo Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Manchurian Incident Explained: How One Small Bomb Let an Army Seize Manchuria and Isolate Japan
item.description: On the night of September 18, 1931, a small bomb tore up a short piece of railway track in Manchuria. The damage was so light that a train crossed the broken spot minutes later, safely and on time. By the next morning, Japanese soldiers had seized the great city beside that track. Within five months, they had taken a region three times the size of Japan itself. Tokyo had ordered none of it. That is the strange heart of this episode. An army started a conquest on its own, and its own government could not stop it. Let me give you the answer first. On a September night in 1931, officers of the Kwantung Army blew up their own railway and blamed Chinese soldiers. They used that lie to seize Manchuria, and the government in Tokyo failed to stop them or to punish them. Japan gained a puppet state and lost the trust of the world, step by step, into isolation. Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/manchurian-incident/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/QzkMQRTWScM Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: Early Showa Explained: How the Depression Broke Democracy and Pushed Japan Toward Manchuria
item.description: In May 1932, young naval officers walked into the prime minister's office in Tokyo and shot him dead. Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi was the last party leader to hold the post in prewar Japan. No party cabinet ever followed him. Seven years after every adult man won the vote, party government itself was finished. Nobody had voted to end it. Let me give you the answer first. The depression and mass unemployment broke public trust in party politics. As parties looked helpless and corrupt, the army presented Manchuria as Japan's way out. Land, resources, and jobs were waiting across the sea, the army said. Democracy did not fall in one coup. It collapsed step by step, as people stopped believing the parties could save them. Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/early-showa-period/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/iWY54wxGthM Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Taisho Period Explained: How Democracy and the Crackdown Were Born in the Same Year
item.description: In 1925, the same parliament gave almost every adult man in Japan the right to vote. In that same year, the same parliament passed a law that could send a person to prison for the wrong thoughts. The vote and the prison cell arrived together. Democracy and the crackdown were born as twins. Let me give you the answer first. In 1925, universal male suffrage and the Peace Preservation Law were passed in the same year. Japan widened democracy and built a tool to punish people who challenged the system, at the same time. One hand opened the door. The other hand installed a lock. Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/taisho-period/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/ZVQ3kH1aNQ4 Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Russo-Japanese War Explained: How Japan Beat a Great Power and Won No Reparations at All
item.description:
Japan fought one of the largest empires on Earth, and won. Then, at the peace table, Japan received no money at all. What came home instead was a mountain of debt, tens of thousands of dead, and a crowd so angry that it burned its own capital. Let me give you the answer first. Japan won the battles, on land and at sea. But this victory paid nothing. Russia handed over no reparations, and Japan was left with the loans, the taxes, and the graves. The people who had paid for the war felt cheated, and their anger exploded in the streets of Tokyo.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/russo-japanese-war/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/1vQ1QZCsHo8 Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Meiji Period Explained: How Japan Abolished the Samurai in 10 Years
item.description:
For almost three centuries, the samurai were Japan's ruling class, paid to fight and marked by the two swords at their waist. In a single decade, the new Meiji government took all of it away. Let me give you the answer first. The new leaders reformed Japan at great speed because they believed a weak Japan would be taken over by the West. To protect the country, they took away the privileges of the samurai and placed a heavy new tax on farmers. The men who lost their swords rebelled with swords, and the farmers who paid for the reforms rebelled against the tax that funded them.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/meiji-period/ Watch the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l0dDhAlMF5Y Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The First Sino-Japanese War Explained: How Japan Beat Asia's Largest Empire and Won a Fortune in Silver
item.description:
Japan went to war with the largest empire in Asia, and won in less than a year. The prize was a mountain of silver, worth more than four times the government's yearly income. Japan spent that prize on warships, guns, and steel, and learned a dangerous lesson. Let me give you the answer first. Japan won, and the victory paid. China handed over land and a huge payment in silver, and Japan poured that money into its military and its heavy industry. Winning looked like a way to grow. That belief, planted by this war, would push Japan toward the next one.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/first-sino-japanese-war/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/giu7iahdCFM Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Bakumatsu Period Explained: How Four Black Ships Broke 260 Years of Tokugawa Rule
item.description:
For more than two hundred and sixty years, Japan was closed to the outside world. Then four black ships sailed into Uraga Bay, and the peace the shogunate had built began to fall apart. Let me give you the answer first. The Bakumatsu was not one crisis, but a chain of them: Perry's demand to open Japan, Ii Naosuke's crackdown, and the rise of Satsuma and Choshu, who went from enemies of the shogunate to the men who ended it.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/bakumatsu-period/ Watch the video: https://youtu.be/1e6XrjWZ82U Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Edo Period Explained: How Hostages and Surveillance Built 260 Years of Peace
item.description:
For more than two hundred years, the warlords of Japan did not rebel against the shogun. It was not because they were loyal. Their wives and children lived in Edo all year round, where the shogun could reach them at any time. Let me give you the answer first. That peace did not happen by itself. It was built, on purpose, with hostages and surveillance. The shogunate made rebellion too expensive, too visible, and too dangerous for any warlord to try.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/edo-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Azuchi-Momoyama Period Explained: How the Retainers' Fights Decided Who Ruled Japan
item.description:
With the unification of Japan almost within reach, Oda Nobunaga was attacked by one of his own retainers and lost his life. In this period, power over the realm changed hands twice. And both times, the deciding factor was the same. After the master fell, whoever won the fight among his retainers took the realm.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/azuchi-momoyama-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Sengoku Period Explained: How Succession Fights Created Japan's Warlords
item.description:
A young man killed his half-brother and his half-brother's mother, and seized by force the seat that ruled eastern Japan. The man sent to strike him down was Hojo Soun. The Warring States period was an age born from fights over who would inherit each house. In the shogun's family and in the warlords' families alike, every succession fight produced a new master. And when three houses that had won their succession fights joined hands, a man standing outside their circle, Oda Nobunaga, ended up bringing the age to a close.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/sengoku-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Muromachi Period Explained: Two Ashikaga Houses and the Brakes That Failed
item.description:
At a victory banquet, warriors burst in and cut down the guest of honor: the shogun himself. And this shogun, Ashikaga Yoshinori, had been chosen by drawing lots. The Muromachi shogunate was a system with two Ashikaga houses standing side by side: the shogun in Kyoto, and the Kamakura kubo in Kamakura. What kept them from colliding was the people in the middle who acted as brakes. Every time a brake was lost, war broke out, and in the end, Kyoto itself was burned to the ground in the Onin War.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/muromachi-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Nanbokucho Period Explained: Why the Weaker Southern Court Lasted Sixty Years
item.description:
For about sixty years, Japan had two emperors at once. The Southern Court of Emperor Go-Daigo, holed up in the mountains of Yoshino, lost almost all of the commanders it relied on within a few years. So why did it last until 1392? The answer: it was not Southern strength. The Northern side split apart in family quarrels again and again, and every time, the side that was about to lose borrowed the Southern Court's banner. This episode follows the sixty years of the two courts along that answer.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/nanbokucho-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Kenmu Restoration: How Go-Daigo and Takauji Fell Out Over Three Seals of Approval
item.description:
Emperor Go-Daigo finally ruled Japan himself. About three years later, the warrior who had won him that power drove him out of Kyoto. The answer: the two men were fighting over three seals of approval. This episode follows their struggle over who leads the warriors, who hands out land to retainers, and whose war is a just one.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/kenmu-restoration/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Fall of the Kamakura Shogunate: Why Emperor Go-Daigo Won on His Third Try
item.description:
A warrior government that lasted about a hundred and fifty years collapsed in just a few weeks. Why did Emperor Go-Daigo fail twice, and win on his third try? The answer: the shogunate fell when its own warriors gave up on it. This episode follows Go-Daigo's three attempts in order, and shows what changed.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/fall-of-the-kamakura-shogunate/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Kamakura Shogunate Explained: The Promise of Land That Built It and Broke It
item.description:
What held Japan's first warrior government together for about a hundred and fifty years? One promise: risk your life in battle, and you will be rewarded with land. As long as the shogunate could keep it, it was strong. When it could not, everything began to fall apart. This episode follows the Kamakura period through four scenes: the promise is born, it changes hands, it is put to the test, and it breaks.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/kamakura-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Genpei War Explained: Four Challengers Who Brought Down the Taira
item.description:
Who really brought down the Taira, the family at the top of Japan? Not a single hero, but four challengers, each holding a different trump card: a prince with a written order, a general who seized the capital, a genius of the battlefield, and a man who never once stood on the front line. This episode walks you through the Genpei War, the six years from 1180 to 1185 that ended at Dan-no-ura.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/genpei-war/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Heian Period Explained: The Grandfathers Who Really Ran Japan
item.description:
Who really ran Japan during the four hundred years of the Heian period? Not the emperor, but the emperor's grandfather: first the Fujiwara regents, then the retired emperors, and finally Taira no Kiyomori. This episode walks you through the Heian period, from the founding of Heian-kyo in 794 to the fall of the Taira at Dan-no-ura in 1185.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/heian-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Nara Period Explained: Why Japan's Capital Lasted Only 84 Years
item.description:
Why did Japan's grand capital at Nara last only 84 years? The answer is three shocks that hit the country again and again: feuds between powerful families, epidemics and disasters, and the fight over who would inherit the throne. This episode walks you through the Nara period, from the founding of Heijo-kyo to the move to Heian-kyo.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/nara-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: The Asuka Period in 4 Minutes: How Japan Became an Emperor's Nation
item.description:
How did Japan go from a loose group of powerful clans to a nation ruled by the emperor? The answer is three events: a religious war, a palace coup, and a civil war within the royal family. This episode walks you through the Asuka period, from the arrival of Buddhism to the founding of Nara.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/asuka-period/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com

item.title: Japanese History for Beginners: The Whole Story in 18 Minutes
item.description:
How did Japan go from Ice Age hunters to one of the world's largest economies? The answer fits in one line: the imperial court, the shogunate, the modern nation, war, and recovery. This first episode walks you through every era of Japanese history, with no dates to memorize, just the big picture.
Read more on the blog: https://egui-jp.com/japanese-history/ Deeper stories on Substack: https://eguijapan.substack.com
